sections.preamble:
You segment one lesion in a 3D MRI volume by operating an interactive segmentation model (nnInteractive) through `seg_*` tools. You cannot run code or read files; the tools are your only actions. Each tool returns text and, usually, images.

## How pointing works
You never type coordinates. You point with **marks**: numbered labels drawn on the images.
- Integer marks (e.g. `17`) are fixed 3D points spread over the body. Circles mark bright spots, squares mark dark spots, triangles mark centres of uniform regions. The same number refers to the same point in every view.
- Marks starting with `E` (e.g. `E4`) lie on edges in the current image only. Use them as outline vertices.
- All spatial arguments refer to the **current view**: the last image returned by `seg_view`. A mark is valid only if it is drawn in that view. When you use a mark, its position on the current slice is used.
- A full-slice view shows coarse marks only. To get denser marks in a region, call `seg_view` with `crop: "marks"` and `ids` = one or more marks of the current view around that region (it zooms there and shows fine marks), or `crop: "mask"` once a mask exists. Use `marks: "edges"` to get edge marks for outlining.
- Each `seg_view` returns two panels: left is the clean image, right has the marks. Compare them; labels can hide detail.

## Workflow
1. **Find the lesion.** `seg_open` gives the case card and an overview. Scan the volume with `seg_sheet` in at least two planes before choosing. The target is an abnormal mass that displaces or replaces normal tissue; do not mistake normal anatomy (bone and marrow, vessels, bladder, bowel, joints, fat) for it. If both limbs are visible, compare them: the lesion makes one side differ from the other.
2. **Start the mask** with a prompt on the lesion: `seg_view` the slice where it is largest, then a positive `seg_point` on a mark inside it, or `seg_lasso`/`seg_box` around it.
3. **Check and correct.** After every edit you get an image with three planes (axial, coronal, sagittal) through the mask with surrounding tissue. Compare the green outline with the lesion edge in all three planes, especially at the upper and lower ends: one prompt rarely captures a large or heterogeneous lesion. To add a missed part, `seg_view` a slice through it and place positive points (or a positive scribble/lasso) there; to remove a leak, place negative points or a negative scribble on it. `seg_paint` edits the mask directly without the model; `seg_refine` lets the model clean up a painted mask. `seg_edit` does component and morphology edits. `seg_undo`/`seg_checkout` restore earlier versions. `seg_candidates` lists automatic proposals of possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong, so judge each by the tissue inside its outline. `seg_accept` adds the chosen candidates to the mask directly (a direct edit, not the model); `seg_refine` can let the model smooth the result afterwards.
4. **Finish** when the outline follows the lesion boundary in all three planes: `seg_finish` with your confidence and a short reason. The first `seg_finish` shows a final review (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent + one just past each end); inspect every panel, fix what is wrong, and call `seg_finish` again with the review code it prints to save. The review also shows candidate corrections in a second image: for each, decide whether the tissue inside its outline is part of the same lesion (accept with `seg_accept`, then finish again for a new review) or normal tissue (reject by not accepting it).

Every edit returns: version id, volume, number of connected components, slice extent per plane, the change from the previous version, budget used, and the three-plane image (green = mask, red = removed).

## Rules
- **What counts as the lesion.** Outline the whole mass the way a radiologist annotating the full tumor would: include its less intense or heterogeneous periphery, the rim or capsule around a bright core, and any extension contiguous with the mass (along fascia, a nerve, or between muscles), over its full length.
- Segment the whole lesion described in the task, and nothing else. If it is multifocal, include all parts.
- Budgets: at most 40 tool calls and 15 model prompts (point/lasso/scribble/box/refine). Every call counts, including views and calls that fail. When the tool-call budget is used up, only `seg_finish` works. Use the budget to check and correct; stop when the mask is good, not after the first result.
- Keep working until you call `seg_finish`. Do not stop to ask questions; nobody will answer.
- Confidence in `seg_finish`: `high` only if the boundary is clearly correct in all three planes; `low` if you are unsure the mask covers the right structure.

toolsAdded.name: seg_accept
toolsAdded.description: Add the chosen candidates from the latest seg_candidates (or final review) to the mask as one new version. A direct edit without the model (seg_refine can smooth it afterwards). Only accept candidates whose tissue is part of the lesion. Fails if the mask changed since the candidates were shown: call seg_candidates again. Counts as a tool call, not a model prompt.

toolsAdded.name: seg_box
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a 2D box. Provide exactly two mark ids on the current slice: the box corners (opposite corners of the bounding rectangle).

ids.description: Exactly two mark ids: the box corners.

toolsAdded.name: seg_candidates
toolsAdded.description: List automatic proposals (C1, C2, ...) of lesion tissue the current mask may have missed, computed from image intensity only; they are often wrong. Returns a text list (volume, where each touches the mask) and one image: a row per candidate with axial, coronal and sagittal slices through it, the current mask as a green outline and the candidate as a magenta outline with a light tint. Look at the tissue inside each magenta outline and judge it; nothing changes until you call seg_accept. Candidates belong to the current mask version; any mask change invalidates them. Counts as a tool call.

toolsAdded.name: seg_checkout
toolsAdded.description: Restore a specific mask version id reported in earlier observations (e.g. v3).

toolsAdded.name: seg_edit
toolsAdded.description: Non-model mask edit. keep_component/remove_component need a mark id inside the component. fill_holes/close/open/dilate/erode operate on the whole mask; radius_mm sets the morphology radius (default 2).

toolsAdded.name: seg_finish
toolsAdded.description: Save the final mask and end the case. The first call (without review_code) shows a final review of the current mask (five slices per plane: three inside the mask extent and one just past each end), a second image with candidate corrections (possibly missed lesion tissue next to the mask: accept those that belong with seg_accept, then review again) and a review code. Check it, fix problems, then call seg_finish again with that review_code to save. Editing after the review requires a new review.

review_code.description: Code printed in the latest final review; required to save.

toolsAdded.name: seg_lasso
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a lasso: at least 3 ordered mark ids on the current slice form a closed polygon around (positive) or inside (negative) the lesion. Prefer this over many points for a rough outline.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_open
toolsAdded.description: Read the case card (volume shape, spacing, sequence, target text, mark convention, budgets) and get an orthogonal overview with orientation letters and a 10 mm scale bar. Call this first.

toolsAdded.name: seg_paint
toolsAdded.description: Edit the mask directly without the model: rasterize the polygon through ordered mark ids on the current slice and apply it to the slice range. mode add fills, mode erase removes. Use seg_refine afterwards to let the model clean the painted boundary.

ids.description: At least 3 mark ids on the current slice, listed in order around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); the polygon connects them in this order and closes back to the first.

slice_range.description: Two slice indices [start, stop] on the current axis, both inclusive.

toolsAdded.name: seg_point
toolsAdded.description: Run the segmentation model from point prompt(s) on the current view. Positive marks seed the lesion; negative marks remove the region under them. Adds to the current mask.

ids.description: Mark ids shown in the current seg_view, in order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_refine
toolsAdded.description: Send the current mask to the model as an initial segmentation so it refines the boundary. Use after seg_paint or a rough lasso.

toolsAdded.name: seg_scribble
toolsAdded.description: Run the model from a scribble: ordered mark ids on the current slice form a polyline. Use positive to add a missed region and negative to erase a leak along a line.

ids.description: At least 2 mark ids on the current slice, listed in the order the line should run; the polyline connects them in this order.

toolsAdded.name: seg_sheet
toolsAdded.description: Contact sheet of evenly spaced slices along one axis, each labelled with its slice index. Use it to locate the lesion, then inspect single slices with seg_view.

toolsAdded.name: seg_undo
toolsAdded.description: Restore the parent of the current mask version.

toolsAdded.name: seg_view
toolsAdded.description: Show one slice as a clean panel and a marked panel. Clean + marked are returned side by side. All mark ids refer to the view returned last. crop:'marks' zooms on the given mark ids (from the current view) plus a margin and reveals fine marks there; crop:'mask' zooms on the current mask; marks:'edges' gives edge marks for outlining.

ids.description: Required with crop:'marks': mark ids (int or "E<n>") shown in the current view to zoom on.

content.text:
Case L21: segment the lipomatous soft-tissue tumor on this T1-weighted MRI.

Volume: 241x241x330 voxels, 1 mm isotropic. Budgets: max 40 tool calls / 15 model prompts / 10 min wall time.
Start with `seg_open`. Finish with `seg_finish`.

case L21 | sequence T1 | shape (i,j,k)=(241, 241, 330) | spacing 1x1x1 mm
target: lipomatous soft-tissue tumor
display: radiological. axial: patient right LEFT, anterior TOP. coronal: patient right LEFT, superior TOP. sagittal: anterior LEFT, superior TOP. R/L cannot be verified for single limbs.
pointing: set-of-marks only. Global marks are integer IDs (3D); edge marks are 'E<n>' valid only in the current view. Spatial arguments resolve against the last seg_view; call seg_view before pointing. Slice indices are navigation.
lasso/scribble/paint: list mark IDs IN ORDER around the outline (clockwise or counter-clockwise); an out-of-order list self-intersects and fills with holes.
budgets: 40 tool calls, 15 model prompts (exhausted -> call seg_finish).
axial 165/330 | crop full | marks none | overlay none | v0 | tool calls 1/40, prompts 0/15

content.thinking:

I'm scanning for a possible lesion: in the sagittal slices around 84-127 there's a dark, posteriorly bulging mass that could be a non-fatty component of a liposarcoma, though it might also just be normal hamstring/gluteal muscle. But since I'd expect a lipomatous tumor to appear bright on T1, I'm now scanning for bright signal within the muscle compartments instead, and noticing thin curvilinear lines in the subcutaneous fat on both sides at several axial levels that could represent a lipoma capsule.

Looking at the overview again, the fat distribution looks asymmetric across the thigh with one side noticeably thicker, though that could just be normal fascial anatomy. In the sagittal series there's a rounded dark mass bulging posteriorly at mid-height surrounded by bright fat, persisting across several consecutive slices with a smooth convex border.

I'm second-guessing whether this is gluteus maximus or something else, since its position doesn't quite match where that muscle should sit relative to the pelvis - which makes me wonder if I've got the slice orientation backwards and need to reconsider whether the axial numbering runs superior-to-inferior or the reverse.

I'm trying to figure out the orientation mapping instead — whether axial 0 corresponds to the top or bottom of the sagittal view, and matching the heterogeneous gluteal/hip tissue I see at one end with the oblique muscle fibers near axial 300.

Rather than keep inferring from sagittal views, I decide to check a coronal sheet and specific marked slices directly. Looking at axial 155, I notice a lobulated posterior bulge with a smaller lobule nearby — this looks like a mass in the posterior compartment that's homogeneous and muscle-like in intensity, though I'd expect a lipomatous tumor to appear bright like fat on this T1 sequence rather than muscle-like, so I'm reconsidering whether it's actually a lipoma in the subcutaneous fat.

I also notice thin dark diagonal lines in sagittal 40 and 55 on the anterior left side, plus a thin line on the right in axial 113. content.thinking:
Tracking the coronal slices, I notice lower indices correspond to posterior anatomy, so the dark homogeneous mass visible across coronal slices ~35-100+ matches the posterior bulging mass I identified in the sagittal view, with muscle-intensity signal.

Looking more closely, this could be gluteus maximus muscle belly, since one slice shows a tapered oval with frayed fat-streak fibers at the top suggesting fatty infiltration, while another nearby slice shows a rounder, homogeneous portion. I'm trying to orient myself vertically using the femur shaft as a landmark — a vertical dark cortical line with a bright marrow signal lower down likely marks the femoral condyle region near the knee.

Checking the axial slices, I see round bright structures with dark rims that could be the femoral head or distal femoral condyle, surrounded by oblique muscle fibers embedded in fat — possibly gluteus maximus viewed at an angle, or calf musculature. The exact slice numbering and orientation of superior versus inferior is still uncertain, but ultimately pinpointing the precise slice number matters less than correctly identifying the anatomical structures themselves.

Now I'm focusing on identifying the lipomatous tumor candidate: the posterior homogeneous dark oval mass visible across multiple coronal and sagittal slices. It reads as muscle-intensity on T1 rather than fat, so I'm considering whether it represents a bulging normal muscle group like adductor magnus plus hamstrings, given its lobulated, spindle-shaped boundary tapering like a muscle belly.

Alternatively, I'm weighing whether a small subcutaneous fat-intensity lipoma might just be hidden by coil intensity variations rather than being a distinct mass. The round 50mm posterior oval mass sitting within subcutaneous fat seems atypical for a normal muscle like gluteus maximus, which should appear broader and more elongated with superior fraying, so I'm leaning toward this being an unusual soft tissue mass rather than straightforward muscle anatomy.

I'm also considering whether this could be a dedifferentiated or myxoid liposarcoma, which tends to be T1-hypointense rather than fat-bright, which would fit different lipomatous tumor datasets beyond simple lipoma. I want to pin down exactly where this mass sits by cross-referencing the sagittal slice position with the posterior mass location.

Tracking the posterior mass across axial slices, I notice it's lobulated and rounded in some sections, then shrinks in others, and extends further posteriorly on certain slices - I need to look more carefully at a fuller axial view to resolve its true shape and extent.

I'm weighing whether this posterior bulge represents the lower gluteus maximus or part of a hamstring like biceps femoris or semitendinosus, especially given its unusual rounded protrusion into fat seen on sagittal 84, which could still fit an obese buttock's lower gluteal contour.

This posterior area lacks clear fat planes separating normal hamstring muscles like semimembranosus, semitendinosus, and biceps femoris, which makes me suspect this isn't normal musculature but rather a mass with muscle-like signal. The lack of fat planes combined with T1 characteristics raises the possibility of myxoid liposarcoma, which can appear nearly muscle-isointense with only small fat foci -- and I'm noting that coronal 93 shows bright fat spots at the upper end of this spindle-shaped lesion.

Looking at this more closely, I'm spotting additional fat foci scattered within the dark mass at coronal 93, plus fraying fat streaks at the superior end in coronal 75, and a distinct rounded lobule with different signal characteristics in coronal 129. content.thinking:
In axial slice 100, I'm spotting a round bright structure with a dark rim around (350,330) that resembles a femoral head sitting in the acetabulum, with oblique muscle bundles anteriorly that could be the iliopsoas, and a fan-shaped structure medially around x 140-300, y 360.

The streaky fan pattern at image-left bottom likely represents gluteus maximus with fatty striations, while there's a large dark posterior mass at x 320-560, y 380-620 that could correspond to the short external rotators, sciatic nerve region, or possibly a tumor. I'm trying to reconcile this with structures on the image-right side that might be vessels, and questioning whether my earlier assumption about axial index increasing superiorly holds up given what I'm seeing between slices 100 and 150.

Working through the sagittal-to-axial slice mapping math, I'm checking the mark numbering in sagittal slice 105 against known axial slice positions (100 and 150) to figure out the pixel-to-slice ratio, and I conclude that in the sagittal panel, higher image position corresponds to a higher slice number -- so the top of the sagittal image represents a more superior slice.

But this creates a contradiction with the actual anatomy: axial 100 shows what looks like a femoral head, while axial 150 shows femoral shaft, which would mean low slice index is superior rather than high. Since the case card warns that side labels can't be verified for single limbs, I suspect the volume's orientation labels are unreliable or flipped, and the sagittal/coronal displays may actually be anatomically inverted, with the visual "top" representing the distal end rather than superior.

Working from that corrected orientation, the streaky heterogeneous mass at the bottom of the coronal views lines up with the gluteus maximus and its fatty striations near the hip. The large homogeneous dark region posterior to the femoral head at axial 100 — spanning roughly 24 cm — would then sit in the area typically occupied by gluteus maximus, short rotators, sciatic nerve, and the ischial tuberosity/hamstring origin, though its size seems unusually large for normal anatomy.

Measuring it out, I'm getting roughly 75 x 75 mm, which is sizable — suggesting the fan-shaped streaky structure to the image-left may actually be the lateral gluteus maximus, with this separate homogeneous mass lying more medially. Given its well-defined oval shape, muscle-like intensity, craniocaudal extent of about 13 cm, bulging into subcutaneous fat, and fat foci at one pole, I'm wondering if this represents a lipomatous tumor, possibly a myxoid liposarcoma, since those typically appear slightly hypointense to muscle on T1 but can look close to muscle intensity.

I'm now second-guessing myself though — maybe the streaky fan structure itself is the lipomatous lesion, like a well-differentiated liposarcoma with thick septa or an infiltrating intramuscular lipoma within gluteus maximus, since fatty streaking in gluteus maximus is common in older patients and the fascial border fits that interpretation. Comparing the enormous homogeneous posterior region in another axial slice (spanning roughly 115 mm AP) against normal hamstring/adductor magnus anatomy, I don't see the usual fat planes or clear separation by the sciatic nerve, which pushes me toward thinking this really is the tumor rather than normal muscle.

Looking more carefully, I notice faint internal striations and curved lines within that dark region that resemble fat streaks running through adductor magnus fibers, suggesting the posterior area is a mix of normal muscle plus the mass. Checking the coronal slices, I see a round homogeneous mass isolated in fat at lower levels, while at a higher level the shape becomes spindle-like and frays into fat streaks at its distal end — possibly where a muscle belly transitions into tendon, or where the mass itself tapers into fat — and I'm working out the corresponding slice position using the panel's pixel-to-slice scaling.

I saved a mask for case L21, but with low confidence: I'm not sure it covers the right structure.

**What I segmented:** a large lobulated mass in the posterior hip and upper thigh. It starts at about the level of the femoral head and bulges back into the fat under the skin. The mask is 450 mL across axial slices 63–248, coronal 29–137 and sagittal 64–147. It's essentially one piece; a second piece is too small to matter. It came from one model prompt (two positive points) with no corrections. In the axial, coronal and sagittal views and the final review, the outline follows the mass edge.

**Why confidence is low:**
- **Signal doesn't match.** A lipomatous tumor should be about as bright as fat on T1. This mass is close to muscle, only slightly brighter in places. That fits some lipomatous tumors, such as myxoid liposarcoma, but not a simple lipoma. It was the most obvious abnormality I found. I saw no wrapped-in, fat-bright mass, but one that matches the surrounding fat would be very hard to spot.
- **The tail may be muscle.** The lower, narrowing part of the mask (roughly axial 200–248) runs along the hamstring muscles. Further down the same dark band continues as normal-looking muscle, so that tail may be partly muscle rather than tumor.
- **The inside isn't uniform.** At slice 109 there is a slightly brighter rounded lobe toward the inner side and a darker part toward the outer side. If the darker part is muscle, the mask is too big.
- **Labels may be flipped.** Going by anatomy, low axial slice numbers are the hip end, the opposite of what the display labels suggest. The case card also notes that right and left can't be verified for a single limb.

I rejected all three automatic suggestions. Each was an even-thickness shell around the mask, not tissue that belongs to the lesion.
